title: Downtown Richmond through time
method: Curated outlines are placed from today's OpenStreetMap street intersections (e.g. the corner of 20th and Cary) and the dimensions the sources give; they are not surveyed. Era rules match OSM names, refs and tags; the first match wins.

next.note: Corrections made after the 1925 and 1950 prints' version 4 (November 17, 2026), drawn in builds made with --with next: those prints stay as sold until their next version.

about: Each scene draws the buildings standing today that had been built by its year (dated by OSM start_date, else the City of Richmond assessor's year built), plus the curated features below. Buildings since demolished appear only where curated. The ground is today's.

epochs.title: The town plan
epochs.note: William Mayo lays out Richmond for William Byrd II: a grid of squares east of Shockoe Creek, sold by lottery. Almost nothing standing today is this old.

epochs.title: A new capital
epochs.note: The capital has moved from Williamsburg; Jefferson's Capitol is finished on Shockoe Hill, and John Mayo's toll bridge first crosses the James.

epochs.title: The Great Basin
epochs.note: The canal's Great Basin is finished below Shockoe Hill, about 1800; Mayo's toll bridge crosses the James.

epochs.title: The Federal town
epochs.note: The Wickham House (1812), the Governor's Mansion (1813) and Monumental Church (1814) stand on the hill.

epochs.title: Canal and mills
epochs.note: The James River and Kanawha Canal ends in the Great Basin; flour mills and ironworks line the canal and the falls.

epochs.title: Mills and rail
epochs.note: The railroads have reached the city; the canal and mills line the river below Main Street.

epochs.title: Antebellum peak
epochs.note: Richmond is among the South's most industrial cities, its flour mills among the largest in the world, and Shockoe Bottom the center of a slave trade that sends people south by the thousand.

epochs.title: After the Evacuation Fire
epochs.note: Retreating Confederates fire the warehouses on 2–3 April; some 35 blocks of the business district burn.

epochs.title: Rebuilding
epochs.note: The burned district is rebuilding; Shockoe Creek still runs open through the valley.

epochs.title: The first Sanborn map
epochs.note: The earliest fire-insurance map of the city. Its buildings now gone are traced here in the map's own colors.

epochs.title: The 1895 Sanborn map
epochs.note: Tobacco factories and warehouses crowd Shockoe Bottom; the canal basin is still open.

epochs.title: Rail and tobacco
epochs.note: Railroads have taken over the canal; tobacco factories and warehouses fill Shockoe Bottom and Tobacco Row. Main Street Station and the river viaduct are about to open.

epochs.title: The 1905 Sanborn map
epochs.note: The second fire-insurance map traced here: the business district at its densest before the office towers.

epochs.title: The rail city
epochs.note: Main Street Station and the river viaducts (1901) carry trains above the streets.

epochs.title: Two cities joined
epochs.note: The new Mayo Bridge (1913) joins Richmond and Manchester, annexed in 1910.

epochs.title: The 1924–25 Sanborn map
epochs.note: Downtown at the height of the tobacco and rail city, as the fire-insurance maps drew it.

epochs.title: The first skyscrapers
epochs.note: The first office towers rise downtown; Shockoe Creek runs underground; the Mayo Bridge has been rebuilt in concrete (1913).

epochs.title: Before the highways
epochs.note: Downtown before the expressways.

epochs.title: Mid-century
epochs.note: The last scene before the turnpike.

epochs.title: The interstate cut
epochs.note: The Richmond-Petersburg Turnpike, now I-95, opened in 1958 through Shockoe Valley.

epochs.title: After the turnpike
epochs.note: I-95, opened in 1958, runs through Shockoe Valley.

epochs.title: The expressway
epochs.note: The Downtown Expressway (1976) runs along the river.

epochs.title: Expressway and office core
epochs.note: The Downtown Expressway (1976) runs along the old canal bed; the James Center stands on the Great Basin's site.

epochs.title: The Canal Walk
epochs.note: The floodwall (1994) and the Canal Walk (1999) have reopened the riverfront.

epochs.title: Living downtown
epochs.note: The decade before today.

epochs.title: Today
epochs.note: The floodwall (1994) and the Canal Walk (1999) have brought the riverfront back; Tobacco Row is apartments.

features.name: Great Turning Basin, James River & Kanawha Canal
features.note: The canal's Great Basin covered three blocks between Cary and Canal Streets, from 8th to 12th Street. Completed about 1800; railroad yards covered about half of it in the 1880s and all of it by the 1920s (the Kanawha Plaza marker). Drawn whole until 1880 (that year approximate); for what was left of it in 1886 see the next entries. Drawn as still water at its own level, with a smooth bank, on today's ground (see How it's made). The James Center stands on the site.

features.name: What was left of the Great Basin in 1886, between 9th and 10th Streets
features.note: The water marked "Basin" in the block between 9th and 10th Streets, Byrd and Canal, on the 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, sheet 11), its outline read from the sheet and placed by the corners of 10th and Byrd, 11th and Byrd and 11th and Canal, as the sheet's traced buildings are. By then rail yards and warehouses covered the rest of the basin. Drawn 1880 to 1895: the start is the marker's "1880s", the end the next map's year, both approximate. Still water at its own level, with a smooth bank, on today's ground.

features.name: Basin between 11th and 12th Streets, 1886
features.note: The narrow water marked "Basin" beside the track and trestle on the east side of Byrd Street between 11th and 12th, on the 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, sheet 11), placed as the entry above. Years approximate, as above.

features.name: James River and Kanawha Canal, from Tredegar to the Great Basin
features.note: The canal's last mile into the Great Basin. Its middle stretch, between 6th and 7th Streets, is read from the 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, sheet 10, "Old James River & Kanawha Canal (Mill Canal)"), placed by the corners of 6th and Byrd, 7th and Byrd and 7th and Canal. West of it the line runs straight to the east end of the canal's dry bed by Tredegar mapped in OpenStreetMap (w307593380), and east of it straight to the basin's west corner, as the 1886 key map shows it: those two runs are approximate. Drawn about 10 m wide (sheet 10 draws it about 8 m) from 1800, the basin's year, to 1895, the end of the basin entries; the railroad laid on its towpath from 1880 is not drawn.

features.name: The canal's last stretch into what was left of the basin, 1886
features.note: From the basin's old west corner to the water left between 9th and 10th Streets, as the 1886 Sanborn key map shows the canal running into it: a straight line, approximate.

features.name: Free Bridge (the Ninth Street Bridge)
features.note: The free road bridge from the foot of 9th Street to Manchester, opened in June 1873 (RVA Mag; Dogtown Dish dates the span it describes to 1878, after the flood of 1877) and closed after the floods of 1969 and 1972, when the Manchester Bridge replaced it. Built "rather low over the river": its deck is drawn 8 m over the water, an assumption. Its line is today's Manchester Bridge's, which the USGS 1:24,000 Richmond quadrangle of 1934 shows it on ("9th St Bridge", just downstream of the Richmond and Petersburg bridge), from the corner of 9th Street to the foot of Commerce Road in Manchester: approximate. Drawn only in builds made with --with next: the 1925 and 1950 prints (version 4) were drawn before it.

features.name: Burned district, Evacuation Fire of 3 April 1865
features.note: Some 35 blocks burned as the Confederate government left the city, from 4th Street east to 16th Street and from the river north, in places, as far as Capitol Square. Drawn simplified: 4th to 16th Streets, from midway between Main and Franklin Streets to the river. The mills and warehouses along the canal burned with it.

features.name: Byrd and Mayo's plan of Richmond, 1737
features.note: William Mayo laid out the town for William Byrd II in 1737: a grid of two-acre squares east of Shockoe Creek, bounded by the river, today's 15th Street, Broad Street and 25th Street. (Encyclopedia Virginia gives 17th to 25th Street for the original blocks.) In the 1737 scene only the streets inside it are drawn.

features.name: Libby Prison (warehouses, 1845–52; prison 1862–65)
features.note: Three brick warehouses, each 110 × 44 ft and four stories, on the east side of 20th Street between Cary and Dock. Used as a Confederate prison 1862–65; dismantled in 1889 and re-erected in Chicago. Footprint from the published dimensions, placed at the corner; not surveyed.

features.name: Gallego Mills, the great mill of 1854
features.note: Twelve stories, 96 ft on Canal Street and 165 ft deep, at the southwest corner of 12th and Canal: by 1860 the largest building in Richmond and claimed as the largest flour mill in the world. Burned in the Evacuation Fire. Footprint from the published dimensions; position from the marker; height assumes about 3.3 m a story.

features.name: Lumpkin's Jail (slave-trading complex)
features.note: The largest of Richmond's slave jails, in the slave-trading district of Shockoe Bottom: a two-and-a-half-story brick building about 41 ft long, operated from the 1830s until 1865 and demolished by 1876. Its foundations were excavated in 2008 beside Main Street Station. Footprint approximate; position from the historical marker.

features.name: Shockoe Creek (open stream)
features.note: The creek ran open between present-day 15th and 16th Streets, dividing the town. A culvert begun in 1877 enclosed part of it, but the 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, key map and sheets 18 and 19) still draws it open from Broad Street to the Dock, so it is drawn to 1890 (the end approximate). Course approximated as midway between the two streets.

features.name: Richmond and Petersburg (Atlantic Coast Line) approach to Byrd Street Station
features.note: The track from the north end of the Richmond and Petersburg bridge (OSM w710689016) across the Haxall Canal into Byrd Street Station at Seventh and Byrd Streets, the R&P's original Richmond station and later the Atlantic Coast Line's headquarters, closed in 1958. Today nothing of it is mapped north of the bridge. Approximate: one track along the middle of the station's throat, read by eye from the USGS 1:24,000 Richmond quadrangles of 1934 and 1956 (which show the line crossing the canal and fanning into the station yard between Seventh and Eighth Streets south of Byrd) and joined to the bridge's mapped end, about 20 m east of where the maps put it. Drawn with the bridge, from 1838 to 1970 (the R&P's depot stood at 8th and Byrd before Byrd Street Station, and the 1886 Sanborn map, volume 1, sheet 10, shows its tracks fanning in between 7th and 9th south of Canal); the years are the bridge's, not the track's.

features.name: Chesapeake and Ohio approach to the Church Hill Tunnel
features.note: The C&O's line to the Church Hill Tunnel's west portal, by 18th Street just north of Marshall: it left the old Virginia Central line west of 17th Street and curved southeast. The tunnel opened in 1873, collapsed on October 2, 1925, and its western end was sealed the following spring, so it is drawn through 1925 and not after. Its course: OSM's abandoned branch (w169784705) from the junction with today's Peninsula Subdivision south to 17th Street; then the C&O spur shown on the 1924–25 Sanborn map, volume 1, sheet 24, crossing the block between 17th and 18th Streets, Marshall and Clay, between the Richmond Cold Storage and International Harvester warehouses (the sheet fitted to the four corners of the block, to about a meter, and the line set midway between the warehouses standing today); then straight across 18th Street to the portal mapped in OSM (the tunnel, w6036486). Approximate.

rules.note: Opened 1 July 1958; designated I-95 a month later.
Opened 3 February 1976.
Unnamed ramps are dated with I-95.
The 9th Street (Manchester) Bridge was completed in 1973.

The curved link from 8th Street to Canal Street crosses ground that the USGS Richmond quadrangles of 1934 and 1956 show as rail yard, so it is later; when it was built is not known here, and it is drawn from 1957: approximate.

A bridge has stood here since John Mayo's toll bridge of 1787-88, rebuilt after floods (1802, 1814, 1816, 1823, 1870, 1877) and after the Confederates burned it on 3 April 1865; the city bought it in 1905 and built today's concrete bridge in 1913. Every form before 1913 is drawn on today's bridge's line and height, an approximation; the 1886 Sanborn key map shows Mayo's Bridge on this line. Not drawn in 1865, the scene after the fire: its rebuilding year is taken as 1866, approximate.

Hull Street's short span at the foot of Mayo's Bridge in Manchester, dated with the bridge it leads to: Hull Street has run from Mayo's Bridge since the bridge's first years (the 1886 Sanborn key map). Where nothing it crosses stands in a year, it is drawn at grade. Approximate.
The floodwall was dedicated on 21 October 1994.

The Canal Walk's channel of the canal between 9th and 12th Streets, as rebuilt and re-watered in 1999: drawn today only. Its line (the ways below) is drawn in past years as the canal's Tidewater Connection.

The Tidewater Connection, opened in 1854 from the Great Basin down to the Richmond Dock (the Kanawha Plaza marker), drawn along OSM's line of today's re-watered channel, which follows it: approximate. The 1886 Sanborn map (volume 1, sheet 11) shows a narrow channel along Byrd Street here. Its end, 1890, is the canal's.
The canal's downtown end, from about 1800 until the railroad took it over (end date approximate); the stretch seen today was re-watered for the Canal Walk in 1999.
David Ross built the mill canal in 1790.

The Richmond and Petersburg (later Atlantic Coast Line) bridge over the James: completed in 1838, destroyed on 2 April 1865, rebuilt as a trestle opened 26 May 1866, burned in 1882 and rebuilt in 1883, rebuilt on concrete piers in 1902, removed in 1970 (Wikipedia). Every form is drawn on OSM's line of the last. OSM keeps it as an abandoned bridge, so today's scene still draws its piers.

Lines out of use or taken up today: OSM does not say when they ran, and what is left of them are fragments that end in open ground or against later buildings (the spurs on the Manchester bank; the approach to the Church Hill Tunnel, which collapsed on 2 October 1925). Drawn in today's view only, unless a rule above dates one from a source.

The Southern (Norfolk Southern) bridge to Manchester, on the line of the Richmond and Danville Railroad's bridge, which the 1886 Sanborn key map shows crossing just upstream of Mayo's Bridge. Drawn from 1866, after the bridges burned in 1865 (the year approximate); before 1865 it is not drawn. Every form is drawn on today's line and height, an approximation.

The elevated viaducts and the Triple Crossing were built with Main Street Station, opened 1901. Rail bridges over the James (the Bellwood Subdivision and Richmond District crossings) are each one OSM way with their viaducts, so they are dated with them; no source here dates the river crossings themselves (undated: needs a source).
Platforms mapped today belong to Main Street Station (1901) and later: dated with it.

The Seaboard Air Line's line through Shockoe Valley and Manchester: the Seaboard reached Richmond in 1900 (its line from Petersburg, the Richmond, Petersburg and Carolina, opened that year), so it is not drawn before. Approximate where the line shares older track.
Railroads reach Richmond from 1836 (the RF&P); lines at grade are dated from then, although today's alignments are later.
Ramps and turning roads of the interchanges, dated with the turnpike: approximate, not sourced.
Parking aisles, driveways and drive-throughs, dated with surface parking (1960): approximate, not sourced.
Paths are not dated: drawn in today's view only.
Fountains are not dated: drawn in today's view only.
Surface parking, from 1960: the year by which the traced buildings no later map accounts for are assumed gone, when clearing for parking and highways began. Approximate, not sourced.
Road bridges not named above (over the rail lines and the interstate) are dated with the viaducts: approximate.
Roundabouts and traffic circles: the modern roundabout came to the United States in 1990, and those mapped here belong to the riverfront's redevelopment. Drawn from 1990: approximate.

Unnamed service roads of no particular kind (the drives and rings of parking lots, private drives): dated with surface parking, from 1960. Approximate, not sourced. Alleys (service=alley) and named service streets stay with the street grid.
The street grid is drawn in every year, within the town plan while it stands and, for minor streets, only beside a building of the year (streetsNearBuildings).
Any other way (construction, elevators, platforms): not dated, drawn today only.
Natural water courses are drawn in every year.

Dams, weirs, canals, drains and ditches not dated above (the Manchester Canal, the Hollywood and VEPCO dams among them): no source here dates them, so they are drawn today only. Undated: each needs a source.
Basins, ponds, pools and canal beds not dated above: drawn today only.
Piers, bridge outlines and other works: not dated, drawn today only.
Parks, playgrounds, sports fields and gardens: no source here dates them (Capitol Square, Libby Hill and Chimborazo parks among them), so they are drawn today only. Undated: each needs a source.
Cemeteries and laid-out grounds: no source here dates them (St. John's churchyard among them), so they are drawn today only. Undated: each needs a source.
Other amenities (fountains, plazas): not dated, drawn today only.

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol, central block
dates.note: Jefferson's Capitol, completed 1788 (https://vga.virginia.gov/?p=73). Its footprint is OSM's central building part (w366226948), taken to be the original building because it stands between the two wings of 1904–06; that identification is not from the source. OSM tags it 8.1 m; its height here, 26 m, is the roof height (85 ft, three floors) SkyscraperPage measured: https://skyscraperpage.com/b190890.

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol, west wing
dates.note: One of the two wings added 1904–06, an OSM building part with two levels and no height (drawn about 7 m, below the houses around the square). 18 m, under the central block's 26 m roof, is approximate.

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol, east wing
dates.note: One of the two wings added 1904–06, an OSM building part with two levels and no height (drawn about 7 m, below the houses around the square). 18 m, under the central block's 26 m roof, is approximate.

dates.name: Virginia State Capitol
dates.note: The Capitol as OSM outlines it today, with the wings of 1904–06, from 1906. OSM maps it as three parts: the central block (below) and the two wings.

dates.name: St. John's Church
dates.note: Completed 1741 (https://lva-virginia.libguides.com/richmond-maps/history). A one-story frame church with a double-pitched roof, enlarged in 1772 and 1829, with a tower from 1833 (rebuilt 1866 and 1904–05). OSM gives no height, so it was drawn at the 16 m guess for a church; 9 m for the ridge is approximate. The outline is today's, so it shows the later additions in every year.

dates.name: First National Bank Building
dates.note: Completed 1913, Richmond's first high-rise; the assessor's year (1911) put it two years early.

dates.name: The Virginia
dates.note: Five-story apartment building of 1906 (National Register); the assessor's year (1847) is the parcel's, not the building's.

dates.name: Hotel John Marshall
dates.note: The hotel opened in 1929 (fifteen floors); the assessor's year (1920) put it in the 1925 scene.

dates.name: Riverside on the James
dates.note: The fifteen-story office tower was built in 2005; the assessor's year (1920) is the old power plant site's.

dates.name: Riverside on the James, parking deck
dates.note: The tower's attached parking deck. Its year is taken to be the tower's (2005); approximate.

dates.name: The Locks Tower
dates.note: Twelve-story apartment tower at 1001 E. Byrd St., completed by October 2019 (planned in 2017: https://richmondbizsense.com/2017/11/20/58m-12-story-tower-slated-along-canal/).

dates.name: South Falls Tower
dates.note: Fourteen-story L-shaped tower at 111 Hull St., finished in 2021 on a former paper-mill site; the assessor's year (1929) put it in the 1950 scene.

dates.name: The Hydro
dates.note: Seven-story apartment building at 101 Manchester Road, recently completed in April 2022.

dates.name: Shiplock Views
dates.note: New apartment building, five stories on Main Street and nine toward the river, slated to be finished in spring 2021.

dates.name: The Hues at City View
dates.note: Apartment building in Manchester completed in July 2025; the assessor's year (1920) put it in the 1925 scene.

dates.name: Virginia Mutual Building
dates.note: Built 1920–21 at 821 E. Main St. Curating its neighbor, the First National Bank Building, sets aside their shared parcel's year, so it is dated here.

dates.name: Ross Building
dates.note: The Ross Building, 801 E. Main St. (OSM: 8th and Main Apartments, old name Ross Building, 18 levels), finished in 1965: SkyscraperPage gives 1965 and 18 floors, and the Main Street Banking Historic District nomination of 2025 gives 1965 (16 stories): https://www.dhr.virginia.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/127-6031_Main_St_Banking_HD_2025_UpdateBD_NRHP_Nomination_FINAL.pdf. The assessor's year (1925) put the tower in the 1925 and 1950 scenes. What stood on the lot before is not known here, so earlier scenes leave the lot empty.

dates.name: Chesapeake and Potomac Telephone Company Building
dates.note: The C&P Telephone building at 703 E. Grace St. (OSM: Verizon Building), built in 1929 by Voorhees, Gmelin and Walker, with later additions. The assessor's year (1900) put it in the 1925 scene. Its building part (w365156597) takes this year.

dates.name: Federal Reserve Bank building (Supreme Court of Virginia)
dates.note: Built 1919–21 for the Federal Reserve Bank at 100 N. Ninth St.; the Supreme Court of Virginia since. The assessor's year is 1919.

dates.name: Hotel Richmond (Barbara Johns Building)
dates.note: The Hotel Richmond, later the Ninth Street Office Building: its first phase opened in 1904 and it was built out in phases until 1911; drawn whole from 1911. The assessor's year is 1903.

dates.name: Mutual Building
dates.note: 909 E. Main St.: built 1904, its upper floors added in 1912 (Main Street Banking Historic District nomination, 2005); drawn at today's height from 1912. The assessor's year is 1904.

dates.name: Hotel Rueger (The Commonwealth)
dates.note: The Hotel Rueger at Ninth and Bank streets (later the Commonwealth Park Hotel), built 1912–13 (Main Street Banking Historic District nomination, 2005; its entry is 9 N. Ninth St., OSM's 901 Bank St. is the same corner). The assessor's year is 1917.

dates.name: State and City Bank and Trust Company Building
dates.note: 900 E. Main St., fourteen stories, 1923 (Main Street Banking Historic District nomination, 2005); the west tower of today's Pocahontas Building complex (https://historicrichmond.com/pocahontas-building/).

dates.name: Pocahontas Building, east tower
dates.note: The east tower of the Pocahontas Building complex at 900 E. Main St., added in 1962 (the 2005 district nomination lists it as a non-historic addition of 1962: https://www.dhr.virginia.gov/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/127-6031_Main_Street_Banking_HD_2005_NR_FINAL.pdf). The assessor's year (1923) is the west tower's.

dates.name: American National Bank Building
dates.note: 1001 E. Main St. (OSM: American Heritage Apartments), built 1904 (Main Street Banking Historic District nomination, 2005). The assessor's year is 1910.

dates.name: 629 East Main Street
dates.note: Fourteen floors, completed 1922 (SkyscraperPage), as the assessor also gives.

dates.name: Virginia Electric and Power Company building (The Edison)
dates.note: 700 E. Franklin St., formerly the headquarters of Virginia Electric & Power Company, a high-rise built in 1913.

dates.name: Richmond Chamber of Commerce (Eskimo Pie) Building
dates.note: 530 E. Main St., built in 1912 for the Richmond Chamber of Commerce by Carneal and Johnston. The assessor's year is 1911.

dates.name: Richmond Garage
dates.note: The Richmond Garage at Sixth and Franklin streets, built in 1927: a parking garage that does date from before the decks of the 1960s (see parkingFrom).

dates.name: Upper Lofts at Canal Walk
dates.note: No source found for when this seven-level building was built: the listing's 1900 is the assessor's year, the only date there is, and is not taken. Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

dates.name: The Lofts at Shiplock Watch
dates.note: Richmond BizSense describes a three- and four-story building, so OSM's nine levels are wrong, and no source found gives its year (the assessor's is 1840). Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

dates.name: 501 East Franklin
dates.note: An eight-level building whose only date is the assessor's (1916); no other source found. Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

dates.name: Virginia Electric and Power Company building, annex
dates.note: The seven-story annex of the 1913 tower at 700 E. Franklin St.; no source found gives its year (the assessor's is the tower's lot, 1913). Drawn in today's scene only until a source dates it.

leaveOut.why: 28 of its 57 traced buildings fall on the Capitol Square lawn, a public square since the Capitol was built (https://vga.virginia.gov/?p=73), so the sheet's fit (read by eye) is wrong; its other buildings are taken to be out of place too. Left out until the sheet is placed again.
3 of its 5 traced buildings fall on the Capitol Square lawn: the same misfit as sheet 5.
